cases.preview: More than 400 Playwright backend feature tests. Failed tests blocked production deployment.
cases.title: Move the platform forward. Bring existing customers with it.
cases.summary: Modernizing .NET applications meant checking complete backend features, not just successful builds. A Playwright suite of more than 400 feature tests covered business workflows and blocked production deployment when tests failed.
cases.problem: Legacy .NET Framework applications and background workers needed to move to modern .NET, while existing clients continued to rely on the same behavior.
cases.decision: Share compatible code, isolate framework-specific concerns, and run the new applications alongside the old ones. Check behavior before increasing traffic rather than assume a successful build means a safe release.
cases.context: A rewrite would have coupled the framework change to unnecessary behavioral changes. Keeping compatibility explicit made it possible to investigate differences before asking customers to depend on the new version.
cases.ownership: I owned the application migration design, implementation, CI/CD changes, and production deployment. Platform engineers supplied the container-platform golden path. The wider team contributed to the evolving test suite.
outcomes: More than 400 Playwright backend feature tests covered reserving, booking, and agency and agent data lifecycles: create test records, update them, and delete them.
Failed feature tests blocked production deployment. The suite checked backend business workflows, not just whether new pods were healthy.
The initial migration moved .NET Framework applications on Windows to .NET 6 on ECS. Later upgrades moved to .NET 8 on ECS and then .NET 10 on EKS.
Response comparisons caught differences that could be fixed before cutover. Later upgrades reused the staged rollout and API regression approach.
During the initial cutover, no HTTP 500s or drop in incoming traffic were observed in the monitoring used for that release.
cases.result: Complete backend feature checks as a production deployment gate.

technical.title: Complete backend feature coverage
technical.description: The Playwright suite contained more than 400 backend feature tests, including reserving, booking, and agency and agent data lifecycles. Tests created test agencies and agents, updated their data, and deleted them, exercising complete workflows rather than only isolated endpoint checks.

technical.title: A production deployment gate
technical.description: The suite ran after staging deployments. If feature tests failed, production deployment was blocked. This gate was separate from the EKS rollout strategy.

technical.title: Compatibility first
technical.description: Shared .NET Standard code bridged the applications. Controllers, dependency injection, and Windows-specific dependencies were handled separately.

technical.title: Validate before switching
technical.description: API responses were compared. New workers initially logged event receipt without sending emails or applying updates, while legacy workers continued production processing.

technical.title: Rolling updates on EKS
technical.description: During EKS rolling updates, previous-version pods were gradually switched off as new-version pods became healthy. Pod health governed that rollout; the Playwright feature suite was the separate gate before production deployment.

cases.takeaway: If an aging application is holding your business back, the first question isn't which framework to pick. It's how to make the change without bundling in avoidable risk.

cases.preview: OAuth and deliberate resilience in one reusable HTTP library, adopted beyond my team.
cases.title: Solve the integration problem once. Make it useful to other teams.
cases.shortTitle: A shared foundation for service integrations
cases.summary: A reusable .NET HTTP library brought OAuth handling and configurable resilience into one place. Other teams adopted it instead of rebuilding the same concerns.
cases.problem: Applications needed consistent authentication and failure handling when calling other services. Repeating those decisions in each application made the shared concerns harder to manage.
cases.decision: Put shared OAuth and resilience behavior into a configurable HTTP client library. Make retry behavior deliberate: operations that weren't classified as idempotent were not automatically retried.
cases.context: Retrying everything can repeat a business action, not just a network request. Standardization needed to preserve that distinction while giving applications control over their client configuration.
cases.ownership: I built the reusable client library and integrated it with the existing OAuth service. Another team owned the OAuth server. This work did not create the authentication platform or make every business operation idempotent.
outcomes: The library was used across multiple APIs and background-job applications in my scope, and adopted by two other .NET teams.
Token handling, timeouts, circuit breakers, and retry settings became shared capabilities instead of repeated application-level implementations.
Teams could reuse the shared behavior while retaining control over the resilience settings of their own HTTP clients.
cases.result: Shared behavior. Configurable boundaries. Adoption beyond one team.

technical.title: Client lifecycle
technical.description: IHttpClientFactory provided client and handler management rather than ad hoc HTTP client creation.

technical.title: Token lifecycle
technical.description: The library centralized token acquisition, reuse, and refresh against the organization's existing OAuth service.

technical.title: Deliberate resilience
technical.description: Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers were configurable. POST and PATCH requests were not automatically retried under the library's method-aware policy.

cases.takeaway: When the same integration concerns keep appearing in your applications, a small reusable capability can be more valuable than another standalone fix.

cases.preview: React for desktop rendering and SEO; Angular for the team's mobile web conventions.
cases.title: Modernize the experience. Choose around the product, not a favorite framework.
cases.shortTitle: A modern web experience for Redbook
cases.summary: A React/TypeScript desktop rewrite supported server rendering and search needs, while the mobile web implementation respected the organization's established Angular conventions.
cases.problem: Redbook's web experience needed modernization across desktop and mobile, within an organization that already had different frontend constraints for each.
cases.decision: Use React for desktop rendering and SEO needs, while keeping the mobile web implementation aligned with established Angular state-management conventions. One framework everywhere wasn't the goal.
cases.context: The better technical choice depends on the product and the team that will maintain it. For this work, consistency with the organization's mobile approach mattered alongside improving the desktop experience.
cases.ownership: I led the React/TypeScript frontend rewrite and delivered the Angular mobile web view as part of the wider product team. This is a description of my contribution, not a claim that I independently owned the whole Redbook product.
outcomes: A modern React/TypeScript desktop implementation and an Angular mobile web experience aligned to their respective constraints.
Server rendering and SEO requirements informed the desktop choice rather than being treated as an afterthought.
The result respected the team's existing mobile conventions rather than introducing a second frontend migration just for stack uniformity.
cases.result: A product-led frontend decision, not a framework-led rewrite.

technical.title: Desktop
technical.description: React and TypeScript, with the implementation choice shaped by server-side rendering and SEO needs.

technical.title: Mobile web
technical.description: Angular aligned with organizational state-management conventions. This was mobile web, not a native mobile rewrite.

technical.title: Full-stack context
technical.description: The work sat within a .NET and AWS product environment. Frontend choices were made with integration and ongoing ownership in mind.

cases.takeaway: If you're improving an existing product, the right starting point is the user need and the team's constraints, not a wholesale commitment to a new stack.
